To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effect of transcription-coupled DNA repair is determined by the number of RNA polymerases that stall at damage sites and that this number is determined by the transcription rate and the promoter strength.

1) The coupling of nucleotide excision to transcription repair in Eschericia coli is mediated by a stalled RNA Polymerase, 2) Stalled RNA polymerases display multiple conformations that are responsible for the coupling and decoupling of repair, 3) The coupling of repair is dependent on the transcription rate of the promoter, 4) A quantitative description of the repair mechanism is presented, and 5) The model can explain the experimental observations reported in literature.

the multiple conforma-tions displayed by a stalled polymerase result in a two-subpathway mechanism for transcription coupled repair and that the model is capable of explaining most of the experimental observations reported in the literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanistic understanding of transcription-coupled DNA repair in E. coli and the implications of this understanding for higher organisms.
developing a mechanistic model for the effect of transcription-coupled DNA repair in Eschericia coli.
the development of an integrated mechanistic framework that can explain the effect of transcription-coupled DNA repair in bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of transcription is not on the repair enzymes per se, but on the repair pathway that is followed.
transcription-coupled DNA repair is not a single process, but a collection of sub-pathways that differ in their mechanism of action and the extent to which they are affected by transcription.
transcription-coupled DNA repair in E. coli occurs via a direct mechanism in the absence of a coupling protein, and via the Mfd-coupled pathway in the presence of Mfd.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

transcription-coupled DNA damage repair is a complex process involving multiple repair sub-pathways and that a coupling protein is not essential for preferential repair of the transcriptional strand of active genes.
the coupling protein Mfd is not the sole determinant of transcription-coupled excision repair.
the model presented here provides a mechanistic basis for the effect of transcription-coupled excision repair in Escherchia coli and higher organisms and provides a basis for further experiments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transcription-coupled DNA repair can be achieved by the direct recruitment of repair enzymes by the stalled RNA polymerase, without the need for a specific coupling protein.
a coupling protein is not essential for transcription-couled repair.
a mechanistic understanding of the effect of RNA polymerase in transcription-coupled DNA repair is essential for developing a quantitative model of the process.
